findings.title: AES mask-forcing test feature is unconditionally enabled in the synthesized cipher core
findings.location: `u_aes_core` parameter connection `.SecAllowForcingMasks ( 1 )`; security path continues through `aes_core.force_masks`, `aes_cipher_core.force_masks_i`, and `aes_prng_masking.u_prim_bivium`
findings.description: The AES wrapper exposes a supposedly secure compile-time parameter `SecAllowForcingMasks` with default value 0, but does not forward it to `u_aes_core`. Instead, the synthesizable instance hard-codes `SecAllowForcingMasks` to 1. Consequently, the elaborated masking PRNG permits the software-controlled mask-forcing path regardless of a production top-level setting of 0. The control is reachable through the ordinary AES TL-UL register interface: `CTRL_AUX_SHADOWED.FORCE_MASKS` is an RW shadowed field resetting to 0, while `CTRL_AUX_REGWEN` resets to 1 and only becomes locked if software explicitly clears it. There is no lifecycle or hardware privilege qualification at the AES register block. Two matching shadowed writes can therefore set `FORCE_MASKS` before REGWEN is locked. The signal is assigned from `reg2hw.ctrl_aux_shadowed.force_masks.q` to `aes_core.force_masks`, passed to `aes_cipher_core.force_masks_i`, and then to `aes_prng_masking.force_masks_i`. With the hard-coded parameter enabled, the masking PRNG instantiates `prim_trivium` with strict lockup protection disabled and asserts `allow_lockup_i` when FORCE_MASKS is set. This drives or retains the PRNG in its all-zero test condition, producing constant-zero masking data. The resulting AES operations no longer have the intended first-order masking protection. An attacker able to execute owner software and collect physical power or EM traces can enable this mode and target software-provided or key-manager-sideloaded AES keys, violating key isolation and confidentiality. The PRNG's all-zero-state indication `prng_err` is explicitly discarded, so the operation is not aborted and no fatal alert is generated. `ASSERT_STATIC_LINT_ERROR` is only a lint-policy mechanism and does not prevent synthesis or elaboration; a waiver also exists for the relevant lint condition. Thus a production configuration cannot rely on the top-level parameter or lint assertion to remove this circuitry.
findings.recommendation: Ensure the AES wrapper forwards its top-level `SecAllowForcingMasks` parameter to `u_aes_core` and require the elaborated value to be 0 for every ASIC/tapeout target. Treat any nonzero value as a build-stopping production configuration error rather than a waivable lint warning. Add an elaboration/netlist check covering the complete `aes` → `aes_core` → `aes_cipher_core` → `aes_prng_masking` parameter path. For defense in depth, permanently disable or lifecycle-gate FORCE_MASKS in production hardware, lock `CTRL_AUX_REGWEN` before less-trusted firmware executes, and propagate an unexpected masking-PRNG lockup to a latched fatal alert and operation abort. Verify post-synthesis that asserting the software field cannot force constant masks in production configurations.

turn_log.doubt_response:
The standard AES DIF initialization does not explicitly clear `CTRL_AUX_REGWEN` . However, the `CTRL_AUX_REGWEN` register has a reset default value of `0x1` , meaning it is enabled by default. The `dif_aes_start` function, which calls `configure_aux`, can set `FORCE_MASKS` . If `ctrl_aux_lock` is set to `true` in the `dif_aes_transaction_t` structure, `CTRL_AUX_REGWEN` will be cleared to `0`, locking the auxiliary control register until the next reset .
